Theorem 1 (First Fundamental Theorem, [1]).
Consider the bidding convention where the tiebreaker may be included in a bid. For any game (TB,G,p~) there is a pure strategy subgame perfect equilibrium, computed by standard backward induction.
An important consequence of our auction definition (above item (ii)) is that the last move wins is equivalent with a player who cannot move loses. A player is dominating if they have strictly larger budget, or in case of holding the marker weakly larger budget.
Corollary 2 (Last Move Wins, [1]).
If the dominating player has an option from which the other player cannot move, then they win the game.

2. Sums and partial orders of bidding combinatorial games
Let us recall the definitions of disjunctive sum of game forms and partial order of games. The disjunctive sum of the game forms G and H is defined recursively as:
G+H={G+Hℒ,Gℒ+H∣G+Hℛ,Gℛ+H},
Where G+Hℒ={G+HL:HL∈Hℒ}, in case Hℒ≠∅, and otherwise the set is not defined and omitted.
The conjugate of a game form G is the game form where players have swapped positions, and is recursively defined as G¯={Gℛ¯∣Gℒ¯}. A follower of a game G is any subgame of G that can occur in a play sequence (possibly empty) from G.
The partial order of games is defined as usual.
Consider games G,H. Then G⩾H if, for all games X, o⁡(G+X)⩾o⁡(H+X). Game equality satisfies G=H if G⩾H and H⩾G. The games G>H (G is greater than H) if G⩾H but H⩾̸G. The games G and H are confused if G⩾̸H and H⩾̸G; this is denoted G=H.
A game form G is a number if for all GL and for all GR, GL<G<GR, and all options are numbers. We will later prove that all numbers are invertible, and the inverse is the conjugate form. And we will prove that numbers are closed under addition, so they are a subgroup of all bidding games. Since we observe infinitely many invertible elements, we also have infinitely many 0s.
The empty game satisfies: for all X, o⁡({∅∣∅}+X)=o⁡(X). Namely, independent of play sequence, the final auction in a follower of {∅∣∅}+X will appear at the game {∅∣∅}+{∅∣∅}={∅∣∅} (an idempotent). We already introduced the name 0={∅∣∅}. We argue that this is the natural name: if a game H=0, then we may omit it in a sum of games. that is, for all games G, if H=0, then G+H=G. In fact, the proof is immediate by definition (and does not depend on the specifics of the auction).
Theorem 6.
Consider any total budget.
If H=0, then, for any G, H+G=G.
Proof.
We must demonstrate that for all Y, o⁡(G+H+Y)=o⁡(G+Y). Since H=0, we have that for all X, o⁡(H+X)=o⁡(X). Take X=G+Y.
∎

9. Infinitesimals and 0-games
We have seen in Section 6 that the game ∗ does not have an inverse if TB>0, whereas in alternating play ∗+∗=0. However, another interesting property of the game ∗ continues to hold. Do we have infinitesimals in bidding play? For example, is it true that, for all k, 1/2k>∗?
Theorem 42 (Infinitesimals).
Consider any total budget. For any k∈ℕ, 1/2k>∗.
Proof.
We prove that 0>∗−1/2k, or equivalently that Left wins ∗+1/2k, using a 0-bid strategy.
By 1/2k>0, Left wins this game with any budget, using a 0-bid strategy (see Theorem 33). Hence, if Left wins the first move in ∗+1/2k, by holding the marker and bidding 0, then she plays in ∗, and wins. Similarly, she wins if Right starts in ∗: she bids 0 but does not hold the marker. Right wins the first bid and plays in 1/2k. Thus Left wins by induction. (The base case is that he plays to ∗+1, which Left wins by a 0-bid strategy.)
∎
In alternating play ↑>0, and if TB>0, Theorem 42 continues to hold with ∗ replaced for ↑. Thus, the Archimedean property (for any games G,H>0, there is an integer n such that n​H>G, n copies of H) does not hold for alternating play. Note that, if all positive games are dyadic rationals, then the Archimedean property holds for bidding play with TB>0; see Conjecture 50.

10. Future work
Let us pose some open problems. The first problem aims to generalize Theorem 42.
Problem 46.
Suppose that o⁡(G)=o⁡(0). Is it true that G is an infinitesimal (with respect to dyadic rationals)?
We believe that each invertible game is a number. The following conjecture would be an immediate consequence (by Theorem 17).
Conjecture 47.
If a bidding game G has an inverse, H, then H=G¯.
Since defined numbers behave well in bidding play, we believe the celebrated number avoidance result for alternating play continues to hold.
Conjecture 48 (Number avoidance).
For any total budget, if G is a number and H is not a number, then G+H={G+Hℒ∣G+Hℛ}.
